notes: Justice (Isekai 825 Rank Progression — Holdings and Powers.md, 'Justice'; 03_HISTORY §10b). One to two cases a year on average, never more than one a season, and none forced: a quiet year is a well-behaved villa, and the many small matters were handled without the lord. Aldric brings the case (Ermenald one with the church in it), the lord judges in talk, the speaker emits justice_verdict from the closed list. At Count and above the lord also sets a stance for the officers who judge in his name; the fines of the office follow it.

lenient.word: lenient: half the fines, the people warm to you two a year, the church approves; disorder grows

fair.word: fair: the fines as custom sets them, the people warm to you one a year; the slow, safe way

strict.word: strict: fines a third above custom, the people cool one a year; resentment gathers quietly

extortionate.word: extortionate: double fines, the people cool three a year, the church condemns it, and the king's missi take notice

framing.county: You hear dozens of cases at the county court this season, my lord, and your officers settle most before they reach you. This is the one that will be remembered.
framing.duke: The lesser courts have done what they could this year, my lord. This one could not be settled below you.

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The boundary stone
villa.text: My lord, a boundary stone between two strips has been moved, and both families swear on the saints it was always where they say. I have walked it; the grass under the stone is fresh. Will you hear them?

verdicts.label: Put the stone back where the grass says it stood, and fine the mover
Split the disputed furrow between them and fine neither
Rule for the older family and let the other learn its place
It is a matter for the village; send them away

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The pig in the beans
villa.text: A pig got into Godo's garden and rooted up the beans he was keeping for seed. The pig is Adalbert's, and Adalbert says the fence was Godo's to mend. Both are at the gate, my lord, and neither is quiet.

verdicts.label: The pig's owner makes good the beans
Half the loss each: the fence was bad and the pig was loose
Fine them both for bringing a pig to the hall
Send them away; it is beans

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The dead man's strip
villa.text: Old Ratbert is dead and two men claim his strip in the open field: his nephew, who worked it beside him these five years, and his son-in-law, who has the widow. The strip is yours to assign, my lord; the custom says the one who worked it, the widow says otherwise.

verdicts.label: The nephew, who worked it
The widow's household, who must eat
Take the strip back into the demesne and let them both look elsewhere
Let them settle it between themselves

villa.speaker: chaplain
villa.title: The betrothal refused
villa.text: My lord, a betrothal was agreed between two households and the bride-price paid. Now the girl's father refuses, and the price has been spent on the roof. The young man's family wants the girl or the silver. The girl, I will say, does not want the young man.

verdicts.label: The price is repaid over two harvests; no one is forced
The bargain stands; the marriage goes forward
The price is forgiven and the matter closed
Leave it to the families

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: Tools from the forge
villa.text: Tools have gone from the forge — a hammer and two sets of tongs. The man accused is Wulfhard, who works as hard as any two and has been accused before of things that were never proven. Bernard wants him whipped. Nothing was found in his house.

verdicts.label: Nothing found, nothing proven; let him go, and let the forge be locked
He swears with oath-helpers; if he finds them he is clear
Whip him as an example and fine him the tools
Let the smith deal with his own forge

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The dues he cannot pay
villa.text: Theutbald says he cannot pay his dues this year: a cow dead, a son sick. His neighbours say he can, and that he was seen selling wool at the gate. If you forgive him, my lord, three more will say the same next year; if you do not, the household may break.

verdicts.label: Defer the dues to next harvest, with the reeve to watch the wool
Forgive the year outright
Collect in full; the law is the law
Take the wool and a fine besides for the lie

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The dog and the sheep
villa.text: A dog has killed three sheep in the night. Two men keep dogs that could have done it; each says it was the other's. The shepherd wants his sheep made good and the dog hanged.

verdicts.label: Both dog-keepers share the loss; the dogs are tied at night
Hang both dogs and let the owners thank you it was not worse
Make the sheep good from your own flock and end it
Dogs and sheep are the shepherd's concern

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: Blood at the harvest feast
villa.text: A man struck another at the harvest feast — a cup, then a fist, then a knife. There is blood but no death, and the wounded man will mend. Both were drunk; both have kin. The law gives a composition for the wound.

verdicts.label: The striker pays the wound-price to the wounded man, and a fine to you
Both were drunk; both pay a fine and shake hands
The striker loses his place at the feast for a year and pays double
Let the kin settle it

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: Timber from your woodland
villa.text: Someone has been taking timber from your woodland without leave — good oak, not firewood. The tracks lead to the lower manses. Two households have new roof-beams this spring, my lord, and neither bought them.

verdicts.label: Fine the households the worth of the oak and leave the roofs
They work the days off in the woodland and plant for what they took
Have the beams pulled down and the men flogged
A roof is a roof; say nothing this once

villa.speaker: chaplain
villa.title: The widow's holding
villa.text: My lord, a widow holds her dead husband's manse and works it well with her children. His brother says it should come to him, as the nearest man of the blood, and offers to take her in. She does not wish to be taken in. The custom could go either way.

verdicts.label: The widow keeps the holding while she works it
The brother takes it and keeps her and the children
The brother takes it and pays her a portion each year
Not the hall's affair

villa.speaker: steward
villa.title: The well
villa.text: Two families share a well, and have for forty years; now one has built a wall across the path to it and the other is drawing from the stream, which is further and fouler. The wall-builder says the path crossed his garden. It did.

verdicts.label: A path to water is older than any garden; the wall comes down
A new path round the garden, dug by both
A man's garden is his own; the wall stands
Let them share the stream

villa.speaker: chaplain
villa.title: Within the forbidden degrees
villa.text: My lord, a couple on the lower manses wish to marry and the degrees are against it — second cousins, by my reckoning, which the canons forbid. They do not care; the families do not care; the village is laughing at me. I would have you forbid it. I am not sure you will.

verdicts.label: Forbid it; the Church's rule is the rule
Allow it and let Ermenald write to the bishop if he must
Send to the bishop for a dispensation, and a gift with the letter
Say nothing either way

county.speaker: steward
county.title: A killing between noble houses
county.text: A man of one noble house has killed a man of another on the road to Beaune. Both houses demand justice at your court and neither will take a wergild: the one wants the killer's head, the other says it was a fair fight. Their men are at the door with swords.

verdicts.label: Set the wergild yourself, high, and make both swear peace on relics
Hang the killer; a death for a death
Exile the killer a year and a day and let the houses cool
Refuse the case and let them fight it out

county.speaker: chaplain
county.title: The abbey's charter and the lord's possession
county.text: An abbey and a lay lord both claim a villa near Saulieu. The abbey has a charter — I have read it, my lord, and the seal is good. The lord has held it for twenty years and his tenants know no other. The law favours the charter; the country favours the man who is there.

verdicts.label: The charter stands; the abbey has the villa
Twenty years' possession is title enough; the lord keeps it
The lord keeps it and pays the abbey a rent for it
Send it to the king's court

county.speaker: steward
county.title: Three brothers and one inheritance
county.text: A dead lord's lands fall to three brothers, and they cannot divide them. The youngest is your own sworn man, my lord, and he looks to you. The eldest says the custom gives him the hall; the middle one says the custom gives them equal parts. Each has a lawyer and all three have men.

verdicts.label: Equal parts, by lot, with the hall to the eldest
The best third to your own man, since he will hold it well
The eldest takes the hall and the lion's share, as the old custom says
Let the brothers settle it

county.speaker: steward
county.title: A vassal accused by his own tenants
county.text: Tenants of one of your sworn men have come to the court over his head: he takes more than his due, they say, a third again above the custom, and beats those who complain. He says they are liars and that it is no business of the count's what passes between a lord and his men. It is, my lord; that is what a count is for. But he is yours.

verdicts.label: Hear the tenants, fix the dues in writing and fine him the excess
Back your man and send the tenants home
A quiet word with him, and the dues set right without a fine
Refuse to hear it

county.speaker: steward
county.title: The robbed merchant
county.text: A merchant was robbed on the road below Avallon — the road is yours to keep safe, and he knows the law that says so. He wants you to make good his loss: forty pounds of pepper and a mule. He has witnesses. He is also, I will say, not a man I would lend to.

verdicts.label: Make good the loss and set a watch on the road
Half his claim, and the watch
He travelled unarmed in a bad year; the loss is his
Send him to the king

county.speaker: steward
county.title: A man who says he is free
county.text: A man says he is free and his lord says he is not. The man's father, he says, was freed by charter; the charter is lost, burned in a raid. The lord says there never was one. There are old men who remember the father as free, and old men who remember otherwise.

verdicts.label: Free, on the oath of the old men who say so
No charter, no freedom; he goes back to his lord
Set a price for his freedom and let him work it off
Refuse to judge without the charter

county.speaker: chaplain
county.title: The bishop's advocate and the count's officer
county.text: My lord, the bishop's advocate and your own officer each claim the right to judge the village of Montcenis. The bishop has an immunity, old and real; your officer says the village was never in it. If you rule for the bishop you lose the pleas of a village; if you rule for your officer you make an enemy at Autun.

verdicts.label: The immunity stands; the bishop's man judges there
Your officer judges; let the bishop write to Rome
The bishop judges the clergy, your man the rest
Leave it as it stands

county.speaker: steward
county.title: The disputed mill
county.text: A lord has built a mill on the river above the old one, and the old miller's wheel runs slow. Both want the right to grind for the villages between them; the villages want the nearer mill. There is money in this, my lord, and whichever way you rule one of them will owe you.

verdicts.label: Both mills stand; the villages grind where they please
The old mill has the right; the new one pays him for the water it takes
The new mill stands and the old miller may pull his wheel
Both stand, and both pay the count a mill-fee for the river

county.speaker: chaplain
county.title: Sorcery
county.text: My lord, a village has brought a woman to the court accused of sorcery: cattle dead, a child sick, words muttered at a gate. I have spoken with her. She is old and sharp-tongued and I do not think she has killed anything. The village is certain, and frightened, and that is the danger.

verdicts.label: No proof; she goes free under the priest's protection
The ordeal of water, as the village demands
Send her to a convent, for her safety and theirs
Refuse the case

county.speaker: steward
county.title: A royal vassal refuses your court
county.text: A royal vassal with lands in the county has been summoned over a boundary and refuses your court entirely: he answers to the king, he says, and not to any count. He is within his rights, perhaps. He is also making you look small before the whole county.

verdicts.label: Write to the king and ask him to send the man to your court
Distrain his cattle until he comes
Let it go; the boundary can wait
Say nothing and let the county talk

duke.speaker: steward
duke.title: Two counts over a border district
duke.text: Two of your counts are in open quarrel over a district on their border; both have armed men out, and there has been a burning. Each asks you to confirm him. Whichever you choose, the other will remember it; if you choose neither, they will settle it with fire.

verdicts.label: Divide the district by the river and make both swear to it before you
Confirm the stronger; he is more use to you
Take the district into your own hand until they can behave
Let them fight

duke.speaker: steward
duke.title: An appeal against your own officer
duke.text: An appeal has come up against one of your own officers, accused of extortion in the pleas: fines doubled, bribes taken, a man kept in irons until his family paid. I believe it, my lord. Judging against him costs you a servant who has been useful; judging for him costs you the county's trust.

verdicts.label: Dismiss him, repay what can be traced and fine him the rest
Keep him and send the appellants home
Move him to another county and repay the appellants quietly
Refuse to hear an appeal against your own man

duke.speaker: chaplain
duke.title: A bishop against a count
duke.text: My lord, a bishop and one of your counts are at law over a church's lands, and the bishop has let it be known that Rome may hear of it if your court does him wrong. The count has the lands and the count has your trust. The bishop has the law, and a long memory.

verdicts.label: The church's lands to the church
The count holds them; let Rome write
The count holds them of the bishop and does homage for them
Send it to Rome yourself

duke.speaker: chaplain
duke.title: A monastery asks immunity
duke.text: My lord, a monastery in your lands asks you to confirm its immunity: freedom from your own officers' jurisdiction, its own courts, its own dues. Every great house has one. To grant it costs you the pleas of a dozen villages; to refuse it is to be the one duke who would not.

verdicts.label: Grant the immunity in full
Grant it for the monks' own lands, not the villages
Refuse; the duke's law runs everywhere
Grant it for a gift to the ducal chest

duke.speaker: steward
duke.title: A disputed succession
duke.text: A count is dead and his son and his brother both claim the county; both parties' men are gathering, and the county's lords are choosing sides. The son is a boy; the brother is a soldier. The custom is the son's. The peace of the county may be the brother's.

verdicts.label: The son, with the brother as his guardian until he is of age
The brother; a county needs a man
The son, and the brother sent away
Let the county's lords choose

duke.speaker: steward
duke.title: A case the king has sent you
duke.text: The king has sent a case down to you to decide: a royal vassal against one of your own counts, over a forest both claim. The king's letter says he trusts your judgement. It is a test, my lord, of whether you will rule in his interest or your own, and he will read the answer either way.

verdicts.label: Rule for the king's man; the forest was the fisc's
Rule for your own count
Divide the forest and send the king the hunting rights
Send it back to the king undecided
